extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) handling design patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patentability and drafting/examining design patent applications under 35 U.S.C. §§ 103 and 112, including obviousness, prior art scope, enablement, new matter, and claim definiteness. Targets examination practice and applicant responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic factual inquiries guiding the evaluation of obviousness are applicable to design patentability: (A) Determining the scope and content of the prior art; (B) Ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; (C) Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (D) Evaluating any objective evidence of nonobviousness (i.e., so‑called 'secondary considerations').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four factual inquiries (from Graham v. John Deere) as the starting framework when evaluating obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) for designs. Each inquiry must be developed in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the prior art — analogous arts
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of relevant prior art for evaluating obviousness extends to all 'analogous arts.' Whether references are analogous in the design context depends not only on mechanical relation but whether the appearance of ornamental features in one suggests application to the other (In re Glavas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the problem is giving an attractive appearance to a surface, it is immaterial whether the surface is wallpaper, oven door, or crockery — ornamentation can be analogous across articles. Conversely, where differences are in shape/form, the nature of the articles must be considered. Apply In re Glavas guidance when assessing analogous arts for designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between prior art and claimed design — overall appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining patentability under 35 U.S.C. 103(a), it is the overall appearance of the design that must be considered. Mere fact of differences is insufficient; differences that are de minimis or inconsequential from a design viewpoint should be identified and explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All differences between the claimed design and the closest reference should be identified in a rejection. If differences are minor with no effect on overall aesthetic appearance, the rejection should state that. Case law (e.g., In re Leslie, In re Lamb) emphasizes similarity of overall appearance as the test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill — designer perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness must be assessed from the viewpoint of a 'designer having ordinary skill in the art' to which the subject matter pertains; courts have described this as the perspective of the 'designer of ... articles of the types presented.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When articulating obviousness, frame what would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill in the specific article type claimed (see In re Nalbandian, In re Carter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective evidence of nonobviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary considerations (e.g., commercial success, copying, expert testimony) are relevant to obviousness and may rebut a prima facie case. Such evidence must be evaluated for probative value and nexus to the ornamental design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider secondary evidence either at the prima facie stage or as rebuttal. Evaluate commercial success for objective evidence and nexus to the design; require expert testimony to establish credentials and avoid legal conclusions; treat copying carefully because it may be attributable to other causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie obviousness standard for designs
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish prima facie obviousness, all claim limitations must be taught or suggested by the prior art. The proper standard is whether the design would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill in the claimed type of article. A basic reference must have an appearance substantially the same as the claimed design; otherwise no holding of obviousness can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed design 'as a whole' to a reference that exists (not a constructed combination of features) — 'design characteristics' means overall visual appearance. Absent a primary reference with substantially the same overall appearance, obviousness over single or combined references is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional or hidden features cannot support patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Features of the design which are functional and/or hidden during end use may not be relied upon to support patentability; a design must be ornamental and visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant attempts to rely on functional/hidden features, examiners must provide evidence supporting prima facie functionality. If applicant wishes to rely on such features for ornamentality, the same ornamentality standard under 35 U.S.C. 171 must be applied (see MPEP § 1504.01(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: When combining references, both must be analogous if configuration changes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a modification to a basic reference involves a change in configuration, both the basic and secondary references must be from analogous arts; the ornamental features must be closely related so a designer would be motivated to combine them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use In re Glavas and related case law: a designer is charged with knowledge of related art; combination proper only if appearance of ornamental features in one suggests application to the other. If modification would destroy the primary reference's broad function, combination is not proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining prior art references — suggestion-to-combine test
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary references may be considered only if there is some suggestion in the prior art to modify the basic design with features from secondary references; the long-standing test is whether the references are so related that the appearance of certain ornamental features in one would suggest their application to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Borden, In re Glavas and related decisions when analyzing whether a combination of references is permissible and whether a designer of ordinary skill would have been motivated to modify the basic reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface-only modifications may relax analogous-art requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When modifying the surface of a basic reference merely to provide an attractive appearance (no change in configuration), it is immaterial whether the secondary reference is analogous art because the modification does not change configuration or destroy characteristics of the basic reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this principle when the proposed change is purely ornamental surface treatment; analogy is less strict for surface ornamentation (In re Glavas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal of prima facie case — applicant's burden and admissible evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a prima facie case of obviousness is established, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut it with objective evidence of nonobviousness. Evidence may include commercial success, expert testimony, copying, and affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must consider any objective evidence submitted. Affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 must show nexus and probative value; see MPEP § 716–716.06 for additional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success requires nexus to the ornamental design
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of commercial success must demonstrate an objective success and that the success can be attributed to the ornamental features of the design; absent nexus, affidavits under 37 CFR 1.132 have minimal evidentiary value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sales data, marketing, and any evidence tying purchaser demand to the claimed ornamental design. See Litton System v. Whirlpool and Avia v. L.A. Gear for precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony evidentiary requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony must establish the professional credentials of the person signing the affidavit/declaration and should not express an opinion on the ultimate legal issue of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that expert submissions avoid legal conclusions and instead provide factual, technical support; cite Avia Group and Panduit decisions for limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying evidence must show significance beyond mere copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying of the design by others is relevant but more than mere evidence of copying is necessary; copying may be attributable to other factors (e.g., contempt for patentee's enforcement ability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek proof that copying was motivated by the design's attractiveness or commercial effect rather than unrelated reasons; evaluate market context and motives (Cable Electric v. Genmark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph usage for 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardized form paragraphs are provided for rejecting claims under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) (single or multiple references), for repeating rejections, final rejections, and rationale language focusing on overall appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specified form paragraphs (¶¶ 15.18, 15.19, 15.67–15.40 series) and insert appropriate bracketed information (reference IDs, reasons). Emphasize that unobviousness must be in overall appearance rather than minute details.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112: drawings are incorporated into the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawing in a design application is incorporated into the claim by use of the claim language 'as shown'; the drawing disclosure can be supplemented by narrative description and is incorporated by 'as shown and described.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that claim scope is defined by what is shown in full lines in the drawings plus any written description. The title does not define scope; it merely identifies the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement and scope — limit to surfaces shown in full lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of a claimed design is limited to those surfaces or portions of the article shown in the drawing in full lines in combination with any additional written description in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on the title to define scope. It is prima facie evidence that omitted surfaces form no part of the claimed design. If visible surfaces are omitted, applicants should add statements clarifying that omitted surfaces form no part of the claimed design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only visible surfaces at point of sale/use must be disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: Only those surfaces of the article that are visible at the point of sale or during use must be disclosed to meet enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112 for design patents; the drawing should illustrate the design as it will appear to purchasers and users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hidden or non-claimed surfaces need not be described. If visible surfaces that are flat and unornamented are considered part of the design, include special description in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistencies among views — nonenabling disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: When inconsistencies among the drawing views are so great that the overall appearance of the design is unclear, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, as nonenabling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Otherwise inconsistencies should be objected to and corrected by applicant. Use form paragraph ¶ 15.20.01 for nonenabling rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion to submit enlarged sketches/photographs to overcome enablement rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may suggest that applicant submit large, clear sketches or photographs showing unclear areas so the examiner can determine if the claim may be clarified without adding new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ¶ 15.20.02 to request specific illustrations; identify unclear areas in the bracketed text.

rubrics_metrics.name: New matter prohibition — amendments must have antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: New matter is subject matter with no antecedent basis in the original specification, drawings or claim. An amendment to a claim without antecedent basis introduces new matter and must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments changing configuration (including removal of three-dimensional surface treatment integral to configuration) introduce prohibited new matter (37 CFR 1.121(a)(6)). Superimposed surface-treatment removals may be permitted only if the underlying configuration was clearly disclosed originally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments to title and disclosure must have antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to the title directed to the article in which the design is embodied must have antecedent basis in the original application; otherwise they result in a written‑description rejection or objection for new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between title amendments directed to the article (may cause 35 U.S.C. 112 rejection) versus environment amendments (may be objected to under 37 CFR 1.121).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible and impermissible amendments examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissible: preliminary amendment filed with application and identified in the oath/declaration; inclusion of a disclaimer in the original filing. Impermissible: amendment to the claim without antecedent basis that changes the configuration or surface appearance by adding previously undisclosed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before entering post‑filing amendments, assess whether the change departs from original configuration or introduces new matter; use case examples (In re Berkman, In re Salmon, In re Daniels) for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph — definiteness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Defects in claim language give rise to a rejection under the second paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112. Definiteness must be analyzed in light of the prior art and application disclosure as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases such as 'or similar article' or 'or the like' have been held indefinite (Ex parte Pappas), though such language in a title directed to environment may not always merit rejection. Evaluate definiteness on facts and circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness when title fails to specify a known article of manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim should be rejected as indefinite when the designation of the design (title and drawings) is such that it cannot be determined what article of manufacture is being claimed (e.g., a design claimed as a 'widget' that does not identify a known article).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ¶ 15.22.03 when the title and disclosure do not inherently identify the article; attempts to clarify title may introduce new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for applicant to provide additional information when title ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: If the title of the article in which the design is embodied is too ambiguous, applicant may be required to provide explanation of the nature and intended use of the article so that proper classification and search can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request additional information such as analogous fields of search, pertinent prior art, advertising, or copending utility application numbers; use ¶ 15.21.01 to specify information requested.
